item.content:encoded:
Ismael Zambada Sicairos, alias “Mayito Flaco”

Ismael Zambada Sicairos, alias “Mayito Flaco” is one of the sons of Mexican drug trafficker Ismael Zambada García, alias “El Mayo.” He is regarded as one of the leading figures of the Mayiza, the faction of the Sinaloa Cartel that remained loyal to the Zambada family following the arrest of El Mayo in July 2024. He was indicted in the United States in 2014 on drug trafficking charges.

What’s in this profile:

  • Recent News on Mayito Flaco
  • What Is Mayito Flaco’s Story?
  • What Criminal Markets Is Mayito Flaco Involved In?
  • Where Does Mayito Flaco Operate?
  • Who Are Mayito Flaco’s Allies and Enemies?
  • What Lies Ahead for Mayito Flaco?

Recent News on Mayito Flaco

August 30, 2026 – Car Bomb Attack in Zacatecas Highlights CJNG-Mayiza Rivalry

A car bomb attack in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas, which exploded outside the police headquarters and left at least 11 people injured, has raised fears of a new escalation in Mexico’s cartel wars.

According to intelligence reports from the Mexican federal government, the Jalisco Cartel New Generation (Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación – CJNG) is allegedly responsible for the bombing, which took place in strategic territory controlled by the Mayiza faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. These events come amid a territorial dispute between the rival criminal groups as the Mayiza aspire to consolidate their recent expansion into the state.

What Is Mayito Flaco’s Story?

Mayito Flaco is one of the estimated 16 children of Ismael Zambada García, alias “El Mayo.” He is believed to have been born in or around Culiacán, Sinaloa, in approximately 1982.  

Mayito Flaco was likely exposed to the inner workings of the Sinaloa Cartel as a child. His father’s eldest son, Vicente Zambada Niebla, alias “El Vicentillo,” testified in 2019 that he began accompanying his father to Sinaloa Cartel meetings as a teenager before gradually becoming involved in his father’s business. El Vicentillo was the first of El Mayo’s children to be arrested and extradited to the United States in March 2009. 

Four years later, another son, Serafín Zambada Ortiz, was arrested by US authorities, and a third son, Ismael Zambada Imperial, alias “Mayito Gordo,” was detained in Mexico in 2014. Their father El Mayo’s decades-long period as a fugitive ended in July 2024, when he was arrested in El Paso, Texas. 

These arrests left power in the hands of Mayito Flaco, who, unlike his predecessors, has so far managed to evade the authorities. 

What Criminal Markets Is Mayito Flaco Involved In?

Mayito Flaco is accused of moving large quantities of cocaine, methamphetamine, and other drugs, as well as the chemicals to manufacture methamphetamine, according to the 2014 indictment, which was unsealed in January 2015. His alleged trafficking network ran through Central and South America, and extended as far as Asia—a key exporter of precursor chemicals for drug production in Mexico. US authorities have also connected Mayito Flaco’s faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, the Mayiza, to fentanyl production and trafficking.

Where Does Mayito Flaco Operate?

Mayito Flaco’s base has historically been the southern part of Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa. The Mayiza uses a combination of territorial control and relationships with other Sinaloa Cartel factions to maintain influence over the drug production region known as the Golden Triangle, which is composed of municipalities stretching through the states of Sinaloa, Durango, and Chihuahua. Other areas of influence include Zacatecas, Sonora, Baja California, and Colima, where the Mayiza has deployed armed wings.

Who Are Mayito Flaco’s Allies and Enemies?

Mayito Flaco’s main rivals are the Chapitos’ current leaders, Iván Archivaldo Guzmán Salazar and Jesús Alfredo Guzmán Salazar. Following El Mayo’s arrest in 2024, fighting between their two Sinaloa Cartel factions escalated into the most serious internal conflict in the group’s history, with both sides contesting control over Sinaloa’s capital, Culiacán, and key trafficking routes in northwestern Mexico.

The Jalisco Cartel New Generation (Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación – CJNG) has historically been an adversary of the Mayiza and has allied with the Chapitos, offering money, weapons, and fighters in southern Sinaloa and border regions extending into Chihuahua and Durango where the Chapitos-Mayiza internal war continues. 

Mayito Flaco has formed alliances with other Sinaloa Cartel factions, most significantly the Cabreras, a family-based organization with longstanding influence in Durango. The criminal group deployed to Culiacán to defend Mayito Flaco at the war’s outbreak, according to local media reports. Local reporting in 2025 indicated that Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias “Chapo Isidro,” had reached an agreement with Mayito Flaco. His organization, the Guasave Cartel, and the Mayiza reportedly share an interest in limiting the Chapitos’ influence in the region. The durability and scope of the reported arrangement remain unclear.

Mayito Flaco has also allied with armed wings including the Rugrats, the Rusos, Los Ántrax, Flechas MZ, the Sombreiza, and the Cazadores around several CJNG strongholds, according to media reports and US authorities. 

What Lies Ahead for Mayito Flaco?

Mayito Flaco’s low profile has likely helped him avoid the level of scrutiny faced by Chapitos leaders, some of whom have been arrested. There is also little indication that the conflict has severely disrupted the group’s criminal economies.

Although weakened by the war in Culiacan, Mayito Flaco is continuing to gain territory from the Chapitos. Still, the war has fueled growing social rejection of the Mayiza and eroded the social ties that the organization spent decades building, and Mayito Flaco represents a new generation of traffickers that is feared, rather than respected, in contrast to their fathers before them.

item.content:encoded:
On the Radar: The End of Colombia’s Total Peace?

How is Colombia’s new president backing up his hardline campaign promises?

Is Ecuador closing in on who ordered the most high-profile murder in its history, Fernando Villavicencio?

And does a wave of high-profile captures and kills across the region signal a renewed regional bet on the “kingpin strategy”—and what comes next?

This week’s top three organized crime stories in On the Radar.

1. Colombia’s De la Espriella Ends “Total Peace,” Opens Door to Glyphosate

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government has formally ended negotiations with three criminal groups: dissidents of the General Staff of Blocks and Front (Estado Mayor de Bloques y Frente – EMBF), led by alias “Calarcá”; the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (Coordinadora Nacional Ejército Bolivariano – CNEB), which includes the Border Command (Comandos de la Frontera); and the Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada – ACSN). Separately, Colombia’s government revoked the decade-old resolution that had suspended aerial glyphosate spraying against coca crops, though the government says fumigation cannot resume until several environmental and judicial conditions are met.

The two moves capture the scale of the shift de la Espriella promised on the campaign trail: away from negotiation and toward militarized, hardline enforcement. But as InSight Crime has reported, glyphosate alone has never solved Colombia’s coca replanting problem, and ending former president Gustavo Petro’s “Total Peace” policy risks pushing fragmented armed groups back into open conflict rather than into the state’s fold.

2. Deported Ex-Minister Jailed in Ecuador’s Villavicencio Assassination Case

José Serrano, Ecuador’s former interior minister and ex-president of the National Assembly, was deported from the United States on August 28 and immediately jailed at the maximum-security El Encuentro prison. Prosecutors allege Serrano used his police contacts to help plan the 2023 assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio. He is one of seven people who will be tried as alleged masterminds of the killing.

The case has become a test of whether Ecuador can hold its political elite accountable for ties to organized crime. This week’s InSight Take, Who Killed Fernando Villavicencio? Ecuador’s Reckoning, breaks down the case against Serrano and the other six defendants and its significance for Ecuador’s fight against organized crime.

3. Kingpin Strategy Going Strong Across the Region

Three separate operations this week underscore how central the “kingpin strategy”—targeting the leaders of criminal groups—remains to security policy across Latin America.

  • Jhonsson Pulpo, leader of Peru’s Pulpos gang, captured in Bolivia. Jhonsson Smit Cruz Torres, alias “Jhonsson Pulpo,” had led the Trujillo-based extortion and kidnapping gang since taking over from his father at 17. He was captured in La Paz on September 1 in a joint operation by Bolivian and Peruvian police, with support from the FBI and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), despite having faked his death and undergone plastic surgery to avoid identification.
  • “El R5,” accused leader of Mexico’s Los Reyes, killed in Michoacán. Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, alias “El R5,” was killed in a shootout with Mexican army and National Guard forces in Tocumbo, Michoacán, on August 30. He had taken control of Los Reyes — part of the Cárteles Unidos alliance — a month earlier, after the capture of its previous leader.
  • Alleged Tiguerones leader captured in Colombia. Eduardo Cecilio Vásquez Ortiz, alias “Colombia,” was captured in Armenia, Colombia, on August 26 in a joint operation between Colombian and Ecuadorian police. He is accused of coordinating drug trafficking and contract killings for Ecuador’s Tiguerones gang even after fleeing to Colombia.

The kingpin strategy has been used for decades on the bet that removing top leaders weakens a group. But countless examples have shown that removing such figures  more often triggers a succession fight—and a new round of violence—than it does a group’s collapse.

The post On the Radar: The End of Colombia’s Total Peace? appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.title: Cheap Drones Are A Costly Problem For Governments in Latin America
item.dc:creator: Stella Horrell
item.description:
Cheap Drones Are A Costly Problem For Governments in Latin America

Mexico and the United States recently signed a non-binding “declaration of intent” deepening security cooperation around counter-drone technology, as governments across Latin America race to adapt to how criminal organizations are transforming the inexpensive commercial technology into increasingly sophisticated tools for surveillance, territorial control, and violence.

The post Cheap Drones Are A Costly Problem For Governments in Latin America appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
Cheap Drones Are A Costly Problem For Governments in Latin America

Mexico and the United States recently agreed to deepen security cooperation around counter-drone technology, as governments across Latin America race to adapt to how criminal organizations are transforming the inexpensive commercial technology into increasingly sophisticated tools for surveillance, territorial control, and violence.

Drones now play a significant role in Colombia’s armed conflict, Brazil’s urban turf wars, and Mexico’s fragmented criminal landscape, and government responses are struggling to keep up with the criminal adaptation of cheap, commercially available drone technology.

The challenge is not simply that criminal organizations have acquired drones, but that they have acquired the ability to modify the technology: commercial quadcopters and First-Person View (FPV) drones designed for consumer markets are now routinely fitted with hand grenades, explosives, or surveillance cameras, having been purchased for relatively modest sums—costing as little as US$600–1,200 in Colombia and Mexico.

The rapid transfer of technical knowledge within and between criminal groups means drone capabilities are evolving faster than governments can contain them

Colombia’s Anti-Drone Squad

The scale of Colombia’s drone problem has grown sharply, with the number of Colombian municipalities affected by drone attacks up from 12 to 41 between 2024 and 2025, while the number of illegal drone attacks increased from 38 to 149 over the same period, according to ACLED. In response, the government is developing a projected $1.68 billion anti-drone shield—the Escudo Nacional Antidrones. The multi-phase program is designed to detect and intercept hostile unmanned aircraft  by training security personnel and creating a specialized military unit within the Colombian army. 

The plan, announced on January 16, 2026, is currently in its initial implementation phase, with authorities reporting early successes in drone seizures as well as targeted operations against specialized operators called “explosivistas especializados en drones,” recruited by criminal groups for their expertise in commercial drone technology and weapons modification.

Disrupting supply chains is another measure the Colombian government is using. Legislation has placed emphasis on restricting the importation of devices at specific chokepoints, namely, ports under the jurisdiction of the Cartagena Regional Customs Directorate and Bogotá’s El Dorado International Airport. The restriction of drone imports via postal services and express deliveries aims to further tighten controls, but legislative gaps persist.

In Colombia’s Catatumbo region, National Liberation Army (Ejército de Liberación Nacional – ELN) guerrilla units are reportedly furnishing drones with thermal imaging sensor technology to enhance surveillance capacities around the clock. Coordinated “swarm attacks” and drones hovering over communities serve as weapons of psychological intimidation to control territory and undermine public confidence in state security forces.

Colombia’s approach suggests the government of President Aberlardo de la Espriella is treating criminal drone capabilities as a permanent dynamic of the complex criminal landscape rather than an emerging or temporary threat, and criminal groups are already finding get-arounds. The government has highlighted the development of fiber-optic drone technology used by criminal groups to evade electronic jamming by current national anti-drone capabilities.

Drones as Intelligence Tools in Brazil’s Favelas

Brazilian authorities are increasingly countering drone use in urban areas contested by criminal groups, such as São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, by relying on localized responses.

Rio’s Civil Police have launched the Coordenadoria de Operações com Aeronaves Não Tripuladas (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Operations Coordination Unit – COANT), incorporating drones into police intelligence and operations for mapping and real-time operational monitoring.

São Paulo’s police have prioritized intelligence-led monitoring operations, even experimenting with targeted strikes against drones using drone guns.

SEE ALSO: Criminal Groups Are Ramping Up Explosives in Mexico

These efforts aspire to hinder powerful gangs like the First Capital Command (Primeiro Comando da Capital—PCC) and Red Command (Comando Vermelho—CV), who are reportedly using drones to monitor favelas, enabling them to track law enforcement movements, identify rival positions, and coordinate attacks while reducing the risks associated with conventional, personnel-intensive reconnaissance.

The Red Command and Pure Third Command (Terceiro Comando Puro—TCP) were reported to be using adapted drones to launch grenades and explosives against one another earlier this year in Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. The CV is also in dispute with militia members: in July, a CV drone detonated a bomb in Curicica, according to federal prosecutors, where the faction was seeking to expand its territorial presence.

Brazil’s approach seeks to reverse the intelligence advantage that drones have given criminal groups. But intelligence-led initiatives such as strikes and the seizure of criminal group drones cannot eliminate their drone operations completely. The low-cost commercial hardware allows criminal syndicates to swiftly replace seized equipment, while maintaining territorial dominance.

Mexico Targets Drone Experts

In Mexico, both federal and state governments continue to introduce harsher penalties to prosecute specialist drone operators, manufacturers, technical facilitators, and suppliers, alongside other measures. 

Mexico strengthened federal penalties in 2024 for criminal drone use, introducing prison terms of 10 to 20 years for attacks using drones to deliver explosives or weapons, and 5 to 10 years for manufacturing, acquiring, or adapting drones to transport prohibited materials. Sentencing could run to 40 years if applicable penalties are combined.

In the State of Mexico, lawmakers are considering a proposal that would impose up to 18 years in prison for using drones to surveil victims or gather information to facilitate crimes such as robbery, livestock theft, and dispossession. 

SEE ALSO: Drones Fuel Criminal Arms Race in Latin America

Measures aim to target experienced drone operators, or “droneros,” who are valuable assets for Mexican criminal groups that rely on sophisticated weaponry to maintain control of territory and drug routes, as well as engineers and bomb-makers capable of rebuilding lost capabilities using commercially available equipment.

The Jalisco New Generation Cartel (Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación – CJNG) has repeatedly demonstrated sophisticated drone capabilities in Michoacán and Jalisco, including attacks using improvised explosive devices (IEDs) against rival groups, security forces, and civilian populations to secure territories and access to trafficking routes for a number of years. The group’s technical expertise has also transferred to its allies—the Familia Michoacana, according to reports. Meanwhile, smaller organizations such as the Carteles Unidos coalition have also adopted similar tactics after acquiring experienced operators, illustrating how drone expertise has diffused well beyond Mexico’s largest criminal organizations.

The effectiveness of Mexico’s approach will depend on whether authorities can build the intelligence, forensic, and prosecutorial capabilities needed to identify these specialized technician operators and networks. 

The post Cheap Drones Are A Costly Problem For Governments in Latin America appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.title: The InSight Take: Organized Crime Adopts the Latest Technologies in the Drone-IED Arms Race
item.dc:creator: Jeremy McDermott and Deborah Bonello
item.description:
The InSight Take: Organized Crime Adopts the Latest Technologies in the Drone-IED Arms Race

Organized crime groups across Latin America are weaponizing commercial drones, pairing them with IEDs to attack rivals, security forces, and civilians. From CJNG's drone unit in Mexico to gang warfare in Rio's favelas and ELN surveillance drones in Colombia, InSight Crime co-director Jeremy McDermott joins Deborah Bonello to ask whether governments can actually keep pace with the threat.

The post The InSight Take: Organized Crime Adopts the Latest Technologies in the Drone-IED Arms Race appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
The InSight Take: Organized Crime Adopts the Latest Technologies in the Drone-IED Arms Race

Organized crime groups across Latin America are weaponizing commercial drones, pairing them with IEDs to attack rivals, security forces, and civilians. From CJNG’s drone unit in Mexico to gang warfare in Rio’s favelas and ELN surveillance drones in Colombia, InSight Crime co-director Jeremy McDermott joins Deborah Bonello to ask whether governments can actually keep pace with the threat.

Deborah: [00:00:00] So on August 17th, the US and Mexico signed what they’re calling a declaration of intent, which is deepening cooperation on drone and counter-drone technology. Washington agreed to give Mexico’s Defense Ministry access to the US Army’s digital marketplace to buy unmanned aerial systems and counter-drone equipment. And according to local reporting in Mexico, it’s the first time the Pentagon has agreed to sell drone technology to Mexico specifically for its campaign against organized crime.

Deborah: [00:00:33] So of course, the agreement doesn’t happen in a vacuum. We’ve seen the Jalisco cartel build a dedicated drone unit that has been dropping IEDs on both rivals and security forces for years now. And nationally, IED seizures in Mexico went from just three devices in 2020 to more than 1300 in 2022. In Colombia, illegal drone attacks jumped from 38 to 149 in a single year. So the question I want to dig into today is simply to ask: What is transnational organized crime looking to achieve with its use of drones and IEDs, and what are governments in the region doing to keep up?

Deborah: [00:01:16] I’m Deborah Bonello, and I’m joined by our co-director, Jeremy McDermott, for this week’s InSight Take. Jerry, thanks for doing this one.

SEE ALSO: Drones Fuel Criminal Arms Race in Latin America

Jeremy: [00:01:24] Hi, Deb. Yeah. When you mention drones, everyone thinks of Ukraine now and waves of drones, which have changed the nature of conventional warfare. But here in Latin America, we’re seeing another quieter war going on with the application of drones and sophisticated explosive capabilities. And it’s obviously our job to try and unpack all this.

Is the Use of Drones and IEDs in Latin America’s Crime Wars New?

Deborah: [00:01:51] Right. And it’s interesting you use Ukraine as a comparison. Obviously, there has been a war going on there for some time, and technically that’s not the case in Latin America. So is this use of drones and IEDs something new?

Jeremy: [00:02:08] It’s really not, Deb. It’s part of an ongoing story. And let’s put our audience in, if you like, a sequence, an evolution of events and technologies that shows that this is really just a latest incarnation of an ongoing situation. Think back to Pablo Escobar and the Medellín cartel. He hired experts from the Basque separatist group ETA to train cartel operatives and explosives. And he then used that knowledge to conduct terrorism in its purest sense. He set out to terrorize the Colombian public and pressure the government into making concessions, and he was victorious in the short term. He got extradition taken off the books. He built his own prison and turned himself in to this prison from where he ran the Medellín cartel. How did he do it? Yes, everyone knows about his sicarios and the targeted assassinations of politicians, judges, policemen, etc.

Jeremy: [00:03:21] But the most powerful tool he used to bring the Colombian government to its knees, essentially, was the use of explosives. And there are several emblematic attacks that members of our audience may well know about or even remember. One was the Avianca airline, where he blew up a conventional airline after it had taken off, killing 110 people on board, three people on the ground. And then he also attacked the headquarters of then Colombia’s secret police, the DAS. Massive car bomb that literally ripped the front of a, of a high-rise building. That killed 63 people and injured hundreds. And in Medellín again, he set off hundreds of IEDs.

Jeremy: [00:04:19] Let’s fast forward a little bit more. I remember covering the trial of the Colombia Three, and these were three IRA men who had come to Colombia to train the guerrillas of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, the FARC, in explosive techniques. The guerrillas used that to build mortars, car bombs, roadside IEDs that for a time changed the tide or certainly shifted Colombia’s civil conflict. And of course, the FARC were among the biggest drug traffickers in the world at the time.

SEE ALSO: Criminal Groups Are Ramping Up Explosives in Mexico

Jeremy: [00:04:55] So I think the way to look at this, Deb, is that in pretty much every field you can think of, organized crime has used its huge resources to invest in anything that gives it an edge, an edge in protecting or facilitating its business. That may be encrypted communications, the use of lawyers, and Byzantine legal strategies. Accountants moving money around and hiding it in shell companies, computer programming, and cryptocurrency. Whatever we’re talking about today is just another facet of this. This is weaponry and military technology that transnational organized crime is using to protect its business and keep the state off its back.

How Sophisticated is Organized Crimes’s Drone Technology?

Deborah: [00:05:48] It’s interesting, you know, when you go back to the times of Escobar. Two questions, really. First, I don’t feel like we’re seeing that kind of terrorism tactic and that level of kind of public damage in today’s cartel wars that we were seeing then. Correct me if I’m wrong. And also, when we say “cartel drones,” I think people at home probably think of something fairly rudimentary. Is that still what we’re seeing in the region?

Jeremy: [00:06:18] No, it doesn’t seem to be. They and, you know, you mentioned the Jalisco cartel in Mexico, who’ve been using drones to great effect. They’re not building their own drones, Deb. So in that sense, you know, they’re not at the cutting edge of drone technology. But what they are doing is they are taking the most advanced drone technology that’s already on the market and adapting it and adapting it efficiently and with remarkable speed. So the Jalisco Cartel has actually set up, as you mentioned in your intro, a specialized drone unit. And it seems to move around because it’s been used in the states of Michoacan, Guanajuato, Chihuahua, Jalisco, Baja California. And now we’re talking a lot of Mexico. It’s been dropping bombs that have damaged buildings. They’ve used it to attack police, either in fixed positions or in vehicles. They’ve even hit an Army helicopter with a combination of gunfire and a drone-borne IED. And then in April last year, there were drone attacks in Michoacan using devices with chemical substances in them: gases that cause respiratory distress in residents. This is innovative, scarily innovative use of open-source technology being applied for purely criminal ends. So no, we’re definitely not talking about bags and nails, are we?

Deborah: [00:07:58] We’re not. And I think the difference, if we can go back just momentarily to the comparison with Escobar, I think the difference is a much smaller scale use, but gradual and constant attrition on communities. And, in the context of these criminal armies that we’ve seen, rather than taking down commercial passenger jets. But of course, it’s not just happening in Mexico.

Jeremy: [00:08:26] Yeah. I mean, let’s switch back to Colombia as always, because we’ve got almost all, actually, of the major groups using drones in Colombia. But the National Liberation Army or ELN are perhaps the ones using the drones most constantly. And they seem to have made another technological leap because they’re using drones with thermal imaging, which means they can use them at night. This is for surveillance for the most part, not necessarily to deliver deliver explosives at night, although, you know, it could be used for that. And this is a guerrilla group applying what’s essentially an insurgent logic to support their territorial control. And, you know, we’ve already discussed this in a previous InSight Take, when we discussed the new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in early August. And the use of drones by the ELN is different to Mexico. It does seem to be much more in keeping with a civil conflict, even though President de la Espriella does not recognize that Colombia is in a civil conflict. But if you want to contrast Mexico and Colombia, we see two very different uses and scales and consistencies of drones and IEDs.

SEE ALSO: National Liberation Army (ELN) Profile

Deborah: [00:10:08] And what about Brazil? Because I think we’ve been seeing not just increased use by the criminal armies there, but more of a response from the government.

Jeremy: [00:10:21] Well. Brazil has its two principal criminal armies. The first capital command, the PCC, and the Red command. And they are using drones over, particularly Rio’s infamous favelas, but also neighborhoods in in São Paulo. This seems to be more intelligence gathering. And they are using the drones as an early warning system on police operations. They’re using the drones to map police routines. There has been some weaponization there as well. There was a house hit in Rio. An explosive dropped during a dispute between the Red Command and another smaller faction, the Third Pure Command. And we’ve heard that drones have been used militarily on militia members, uh,their rivals in Rio as recently as July in a push to expand territory or contain the territorial advance of their rivals.

SEE ALSO: Mexico Drone Attacks Spike After CJNG, Familia Michoacana Alliance 

Jeremy: [00:11:40] This again, slightly different use, mainly intelligence gathering, mainly mapping and monitoring of security force patterns and routines. But we’ve seen drones used, I would say almost around the region Deb, around prisons, for example, especially around prisons, to move contraband across prison walls, to get messages in and out for gang leaders that have been incarcerated. And in Ecuador, for example, we’ve seen them using cameras, fixed cameras, along with drones, again, to control territory and to ensure they’re not surprised by security forces. So wide regional use, but the three nations that you’ve mentioned are Colombia, Mexico, and Brazil; all illustrate different focuses in terms of this, the application of this technology.

What are Governments Doing to Address Drones and Explosive Use by Criminal Groups?

Deborah: [00:12:44] That’s right. So walk us through what governments are doing to sort of respond to this. We all, we have seen a pattern of how organized crime is generally a little bit of a step ahead in terms of the way that it operates. What are you seeing in Colombia in terms of what the government is doing to face this down? Because it is a serious challenge.

Jeremy: [00:13:09] Yeah. The Colombians have the most ambition and have spent the most money or are spending the most money on this. And of course they are, whether or not you admit there’s a civil conflict or not, this is a country that is essentially at war. And so they have taken what perhaps we would describe as a more traditional war approach. They have announced and begun to implement implement almost $1.7 billion program under what they’re calling Escudo Nacional Anti-Drones, the National Anti-drone Shield, built in the military with specialized units. They’re also, as part of this strategy, looking to take out the bomb makers and drone makers in the illegal armies. And they’re going after the supply chain too, looking at drone imports, customs, postal service, the airport, etc. So they have gone quite big on this, which reflects the fact that drones are now a regular part of the Colombian battlefield. And they have set up now a permanent unit and a permanent strategy to take on the ever-growing drone threat.

Deborah: [00:14:52] Yeah. And it’s hard, really, to conceptualize amounts of money and what they can buy, but it does seem like a major initiative, and a huge amount of money to build an infrastructure for even a year or 18 months ago was a fairly marginal threat. I don’t know. What do you think?

Jeremy: [00:15:13] Yeah, I think the threat is definitely growing. And ACLED, the NGO that that charts these sort of things has seen in a year drone attacks go up from 12 to 41. And then the year before, 38 to 149. So what we are seeing is a major escalation from the military viewpoint. Deb, they’re taking casualties, and so they are taking they are looking at this as the military look at every threat. This is a change on the battlefield. They need to adapt to the changing battlefield. They need to defend their personnel, and they need to take the offensive. So, you know, this isn’t just them using drones and looking at drones from a defensive perspective. They are certainly using drones now, particularly,on the surveillance front in a much more systematic way.

SEE ALSO: Colombia’s Doubtful Progress Against Landmines

Deborah: [00:16:11] Right.
